overview.title: Resizing the test image for SAM and planning display utilities
overview.main_topic: Preparing the fruit test image for SAM's fixed 1024 × 1024 input by resizing the longest side to 1,024 and padding the rest (`ops.image.resize` with `pad_to_aspect_ratio=True`), and listing the plotting helpers needed later.
overview.central_idea: Resizing straight to a square would distort a non-square image; instead, scale it so the longest side is 1,024 pixels and fill the remaining area with a constant (0), which keeps the aspect ratio.
overview.importance: Correct preprocessing is necessary for good pretrained-model results, and the point and box prompts on the following pages are given in the coordinates of this resized, padded 1024 × 1024 image.
learning_objectives: Explain why a plain resize to 1024 × 1024 distorts non-square images.
Describe resize-then-pad (letterboxing) and implement it with `keras.ops.image.resize(..., pad_to_aspect_ratio=True)`.
Compute the resized dimensions and padding amounts for a given image shape.
List the four display utilities and why they share a Matplotlib axis.
prerequisites: Image tensors of shape (height, width, channels) (p.257).

summary:
**Figure 11.9** shows the test image: two bananas lying on a white marble surface beside a wooden bowl holding a yellow mango and three red-and-yellow peaches (the point prompt on p.348 is described as "landing on a peach", and p.351 boxes "the mango"). The image is wider than it is tall.

SAM expects **1024 × 1024** inputs. Forcing an arbitrary image to that size would **distort its aspect ratio**, and this image isn't square. The better approach is to **resize so the longest side becomes 1,024 pixels**, then **pad** the remaining pixels with a filler value such as 0. Keras does both in one call with the `pad_to_aspect_ratio` argument of `keras.ops.image.resize()`:

```python
image_size = (1024, 1024)
def resize_and_pad(x):
    return ops.image.resize(x, image_size, pad_to_aspect_ratio=True)
image = resize_and_pad(image_array)
```

The result `image` is a 1024 × 1024 × 3 tensor in which the fruit photo keeps its proportions and the leftover rows are filled with black (0). Beyond the book: in Keras the padding is split evenly between the two sides (top and bottom for a landscape image).

The page then lists **four display utilities** needed for working with the model: show images, show segmentation masks overlaid on an image, highlight specific points, and show boxes overlaid on an image. Each takes a Matplotlib axis object `ax`, so all of them can draw on the **same figure**; for example, image, mask and prompt point stacked together. The code for the utilities is at the top of p.347.

paragraphs.excerpt: SAM expects inputs that are 1024 × 1024. However, forcibly resizing arbitrary images
paragraphs.what_it_says: SAM takes 1024 × 1024 inputs. Resizing a non-square image straight to that size would distort it, so instead the longest side is resized to 1,024 pixels and the rest is padded with a filler such as 0, using `pad_to_aspect_ratio` in `keras.ops.image.resize()`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A plain resize stretches the short side: a 4:3 photo forced into a square would make round apples look oval. SAM was trained on undistorted objects, so stretched shapes are out of distribution. Resize-and-pad scales both axes by the same factor $s = 1024 / \max(H, W)$, then fills the gap so the tensor is square.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Matching the pretrained model's expected input format is necessary for good results (the same point the book made about input ranges for Xception, p.282). It also fixes the coordinate system used for prompts: the point (580, 450) on p.347 refers to the padded 1024 × 1024 image.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Letterboxing: scale factor $s = 1024/\max(H,W)$; new size $(\operatorname{round}(sH), \operatorname{round}(sW))$; padding $1024 - \text{new size}$ on the short dimension. Beyond the book: Keras centers the resized image and splits the padding between both sides; the original SAM implementation pads only on the bottom/right, so pixel coordinates differ by the offset.

terminology.meaning: Width divided by height of an image.
Constant pixels (here 0, i.e., black) added to reach the target size.
Option of `keras.ops.image.resize` that preserves aspect ratio by padding instead of stretching.

p.282: pretrained models expect inputs matching their pretraining preprocessing.
p.347: prompts are given as pixel coordinates in this resized image.

paragraphs.what_it_says: We'll define helpers to display images, display segmentation masks overlaid on an image, highlight points, and display boxes overlaid on an image.
paragraphs.what_it_means: These four helpers match the four things to look at when prompting SAM: the input, its output mask, a point prompt and a box prompt. Overlays let you check visually whether the mask covers the object you indicated.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Segmentation results can only really be judged visually, and the later figures (11.10 onward) are drawn with these helpers.

terminology.meaning: Drawing a semi-transparent mask, marker or box on top of an image.

paragraphs.what_it_says: All the utilities take a Matplotlib axis object, `ax`, so that they can draw on the same figure.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Instead of each helper creating its own plot, they all draw onto a shared Axes, so successive calls stack layers: image, then mask, then point or box. The callers pass `plt.gca()` (the current Axes, p.347).

paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book): Matplotlib's own name for this object is `Axes` (a plot area), which differs from an `Axis` (a single x or y axis); the book's 'axis object' means the Axes.

terminology.meaning: A plotting area within a figure, on which `imshow`, `scatter` and patches are drawn.

concepts.name: Aspect-ratio-preserving resize with padding (letterboxing)
concepts.definition: Scaling an image uniformly so its longest side equals the target size, then padding the shorter side with a constant to reach a square input.
concepts.intuition: Like fitting a widescreen movie on a square screen with black bars rather than squashing it.
concepts.technical: `ops.image.resize(x, (1024, 1024), pad_to_aspect_ratio=True)`; scale $s = 1024/\max(H,W)$; fill value 0 by default.
concepts.significance: It keeps object shapes undistorted, as SAM saw them in training.
concepts.example: A 4:3 image of 4032 × 3024 becomes 1024 × 768, padded with 128 rows of zeros above and below (illustrative numbers; the book doesn't give the original size).
concepts.misconception: Padding doesn't add information or crop anything; it only adds constant-valued pixels.

concepts.name: Matching a pretrained model's input format
concepts.definition: Transforming inputs (size, range, layout) into the form the pretrained model was trained on.
concepts.technical: For SAM: 1024 × 1024 × 3 inputs, here built from the original photo by resize and pad.
concepts.significance: Mismatched inputs degrade a pretrained model's accuracy.
concepts.example: Xception input rescaling via `ImageConverter` (p.282); SAM resizing here.
concepts.misconception: Any resize will do; in fact, distortion can hurt.

math.title: Resize-and-pad geometry
math.source_text: first resize the image so that its longest side becomes 1,024 pixels long and then pad the remaining pixels with a filler value, such as 0

variables.meaning: Uniform scale factor (same for both axes, so the aspect ratio is kept).
Resized height and width; the larger of them equals 1024.
Total rows/columns of filler; one of them is 0.

math.operations: A ratio, multiplication and rounding, then subtraction.
math.purpose: Makes precise what the page describes in words.
math.interpretation: Only the shorter dimension gets padding.
math.intuition: Shrink until the long side fits, then fill the gap.
math.numerical_example: For $H = 3024$, $W = 4032$: $s = 1024/4032 \approx 0.254$, so $(H', W') = (768, 1024)$ and $\text{pad}_H = 256$ (Keras splits it, 128 top and 128 bottom; beyond the book), $\text{pad}_W = 0$.

code.title: Resizing and padding the test image to 1024 × 1024
code.what_it_does: Converts the original fruit image into a 1024 × 1024 × 3 tensor whose content keeps its aspect ratio, with zero padding filling the leftover area.

line_explanations.explanation: Imports Keras's backend-agnostic ops namespace (works with TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch).

`ops.image.resize` with `pad_to_aspect_ratio=True` scales the image uniformly so it fits into 1024 × 1024, then pads the short side. Beyond the book: the default `fill_value` is 0 and the default interpolation is bilinear.
Applies it to `image_array` (from p.345); `image` is a backend tensor, which is why `show_image` on p.347 calls `ops.convert_to_numpy`.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: (H, W, 3) float32 array. Output: (1024, 1024, 3) tensor.
code.algorithm: Compute uniform scale → resize → pad to square with 0.
code.theory_link: Preserves the geometry SAM learned from undistorted SA-1B images.
pitfalls: Prompt coordinates must be given in the resized, padded image's pixel space, not the original image's.
The padded area is black (0); masks should not extend into it, but a plotted image will show black bars.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: map a point from original-image coordinates to the padded 1024x1024 image
H, W = image_array.shape[:2]
s = 1024 / max(H, W)
new_h, new_w = round(H * s), round(W * s)
off_y, off_x = (1024 - new_h) // 2, (1024 - new_w) // 2   # Keras centers the image
def to_model_coords(x, y):
    return x * s + off_x, y * s + off_y

deeper.title: Stretching vs. letterboxing, visually
deeper.body: Stretching is like squeezing a landscape photo into a square frame: everything gets taller and thinner, so round apples become ovals. Letterboxing is like mounting it on a square black card: the photo keeps its shape and the empty band is plain black. A model that has learned what apples look like recognizes the letterboxed version more easily.

deeper.title: Why one fixed input size?
deeper.body: Beyond the book: SAM's ViT image encoder splits the 1024 × 1024 input into 16 × 16 patches, giving a fixed 64 × 64 grid of image-embedding positions with learned positional embeddings for exactly that grid. A fixed input size keeps this grid consistent, which is why the KerasHub model expects exactly 1024 × 1024.

misconceptions.claim: Resizing directly to 1024 × 1024 is fine because the model will adapt.
misconceptions.correction: It distorts the aspect ratio of non-square images; the book recommends resize-and-pad.

misconceptions.claim: Padding crops part of the image.
misconceptions.correction: Padding adds filler pixels (0); none of the image is removed. Cropping would be the alternative that loses content.

misconceptions.claim: Prompt coordinates refer to the original photo's pixels.
misconceptions.correction: They refer to the 1024 × 1024 padded image passed to the model (inference from the code on p.347–348, which uses `image`).

takeaways: Don't stretch non-square images: resize so the longest side is 1,024 and pad the rest with 0.
`ops.image.resize(x, (1024, 1024), pad_to_aspect_ratio=True)` does this in one call.
Prompt coordinates live in the resized, padded image space.
Four helpers (image, mask, points, box) all draw on a shared Matplotlib axis `ax` so they can be layered.

questions.question: Why not simply resize the fruit image to 1024 × 1024?
options: It would distort the aspect ratio, because the image isn't square
It would change the number of color channels
questions.answer: It would distort the aspect ratio, because the image isn't square
questions.explanation: The page says so directly. Speed is not the issue, SAM does expect square 1024 × 1024 input, and resizing never changes the channel count.

questions.question: An image is 600 pixels tall and 800 pixels wide. After resize-and-pad to 1024 × 1024, what is the size of the resized content, and how many padding rows are added in total?
questions.answer: Scale $s = 1024/800 = 1.28$: content is 768 × 1024 (H × W); $1024 - 768 = 256$ padding rows in total.
questions.explanation: The longest side (width) becomes 1024; height scales by the same factor; only the height gets padded. (In Keras the 256 rows are split 128/128.)

questions.question: Which argument of `keras.ops.image.resize()` gives aspect-ratio-preserving resizing with padding?
List the four display utilities the authors plan to write.
questions.answer: Display images; display segmentation masks overlaid on an image; highlight specific points on an image; display boxes overlaid on an image.
questions.explanation: The bullet list on the page; their code is on p.347.

questions.question: Why do all the utilities take a Matplotlib axis object `ax` instead of creating their own plots?
questions.answer: So they can all draw on the same figure, layering the image, mask, points and boxes on top of each other.
questions.explanation: Stated in the last sentence on the page.

questions.question: After `resize_and_pad`, why is it important to specify prompt points in the coordinates of `image` rather than of `image_array`?
questions.answer: The model sees `image` (scaled and padded); a point from the original image would land on a different location unless it is scaled by $s$ and shifted by the padding offset.
questions.explanation: Inference from the preprocessing; the point prompts on p.347–348 are drawn on and passed with `image`.

questions.question: Could you implement resize-and-pad by hand (compute the scale, resize, pad) without `pad_to_aspect_ratio`?
questions.answer: Yes: s = 1024 / max(H, W); resize to (round(sH), round(sW)); pad the short side with zeros up to 1024.
questions.explanation: Compare with the formula in the math section.
